summary:
In September 2026, smoke from Indonesia’s forest fires blanketed the Malay Peninsula for nearly two months. Inspired by this experience, we created **AirLab**, an accessible web-based gallery that transforms Earth observation data into music, allowing anyone to hear the air we breathe.

Visitors enter a virtual stage beneath a star-filled dome, surrounded by four immersive, curved screens. Each screen acts as a jukebox, transforming NASA Earth observation data into music in real time: atmospheric aerosols (GEOS), carbon dioxide (modelled on DYAMOND), forest canopy height (GEDI LiDAR), and nitrogen dioxide (GEOS-CF). Each dataset has its own musical language: airborne particles become distinct instruments, rising CO₂ accelerates the piano, taller forest canopies produce higher notes, and increasing pollution transforms bright major melodies into slower, darker minor tunes.

Designed with accessibility at its core, AirLab features a documentary-style narrator, full keyboard navigation, and screen-reader support, ensuring that visitors can experience and explore environmental data even without sight.

Through AirLab, we respond to the NASA Earth Information Jukebox challenge by turning scientific observations into an interactive audiovisual experience. By letting people hear pollution accumulate over a city rather than simply see it on a map, we make otherwise abstract climate data tangible, personal, memorable, and accessible to everyone.
details:
What exactly does it do?

AirLab is an accessible web experience that turns NASA Earth science visualisations into music. Visitors stand on a virtual stage under an open dome of stars, with Jupiter, Saturn, Mars, Venus, Neptune and the Moon drifting overhead. Around the stage are four curved screens, and each one is a jukebox for a different NASA view of our planet:

Exhibit

NASA source

What you hear

Aerosols

GEOS model aerosol visualisation

Each particle type has its own instrument: ocean swell for sea salt, bowed strings for dust, crackling plucks for smoke, glass bells for sulfates

Forest Canopy

GEDI lidar (RH100 canopy height)

Taller trees play higher notes as you sweep along the space station's ground track

Carbon Currents

Modelled on DYAMOND Global CO₂ (SVS #5196)

A single piano speeds up (to ~260 BPM) when CO₂ rises and slows (to ~30 BPM) when it falls; the sound leans left or right with the wind

Nitrogen Dioxide

GEOS-CF 27-hour NO₂ forecast

Clean areas play a lively major tune; dark, polluted plumes play a slow, sad minor tune

How does it work?

  • The planetarium: a 3D scene built in Three.js (WebGL).
    • Sky: over 16,000 twinkling stars, a Milky Way band, shooting stars, and planets with textures generated in code.
    • Moving around: visitors drag or use the arrow keys to turn, and press Enter to zoom into a screen. That jukebox then opens full screen, with a button to return to the dome.
    • Ambient sound: a soft pad, plus chimes as you turn between screens.
    • It speaks one phrase at a time, with its own pitch, speed and pauses, and adds emphasis and dramatic beats.
    • It describes each screen, the planets and every change of view.
    • Map: an interactive world map with real country borders, city and country search, and pin dropping.
    • Flow: CO₂ is drawn as flowing particle streams coloured with NASA's colour bar.
    • Backend: a Python backend serves a 2° CO₂ and wind grid every 2 hours. It also offers an API (/api/sonify) that returns the tempo and sound settings for any place and time.
  • Forest Canopy: GEDI footprints are processed by a Python pipeline. It also includes machine-learning canopy-height predictions, checked with spatial validation (RMSE and R²).

What benefits does it have?

  • Accessible by design: blind and low-vision users can explore Earth data by ear, through narration, full keyboard control, screen-reader support, a list view, high contrast, larger text and reduced motion.
  • Intuitive: each jukebox follows one simple, consistent rule that can be learnt in seconds, and audio guides demonstrate each rule.
  • Engaging for everyone: sound reveals patterns that are easy to miss by eye, such as the daily rise and fall of CO₂ or a plume arriving. It also builds an emotional connection with the planet.
  • Runs anywhere: it works in a web browser with no installation, and headphones are recommended.

What do you hope to achieve?

We want to make NASA's Earth science open to people who have been left out of visual-only communication, and to give everyone a new, felt way of understanding the planet. If you can hear pollution building over a city or a forest rising beneath a satellite, climate data becomes personal and memorable. We hope it can be used in classrooms, museums, planetarium shows and accessibility programmes.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

Languages: JavaScript, HTML and CSS for the web app; Python for offline data preparation.

Front end:

  • Three.js (WebGL) for the 3D planetarium dome
  • Canvas 2D for the exhibit visuals
  • Leaflet for the canopy map
  • D3.js (d3-geo) and TopoJSON for the maps, with Natural Earth borders
  • Tailwind CSS
  • localStorage to remember each visitor’s display and sound settings

Audio, speech and accessibility:

  • Web Audio API for live synthesis and scheduling, including a Markov-chain melody generator
  • Web Speech API for the narrator
  • ARIA live regions, full keyboard control and a text-only index for screen-reader users

Data preparation (offline, in Python):

  • NumPy and xarray/NetCDF tooling to process model data
  • A GEDI processing and machine-learning pipeline that extracts RH100 canopy heights from the HDF5 files and checks predictions with spatial validation (RMSE and R²)
  • pytest for testing the scripts
  • Everything is exported as lightweight JSON and image files, which ship with the site.

Build and hosting: Vite (multi-page build) and Vercel (static hosting). There is no server: the whole experience runs in the visitor’s browser.

Data sources:

  • NASA Scientific Visualization Studio and Earth Information Center visuals: GEOS aerosols, DYAMOND CO₂, GEDI L2B and the GEOS-CF NO₂ forecast. Carbon Currents uses a labelled simulation modelled on DYAMOND.
  • NASA Blue Marble and Black Marble imagery for the 3D Earth
  • Natural Earth borders and Esri map tiles (non-NASA)

Hardware: Standard laptops and headphones. No special hardware is needed.

AI assistance: Claude (Anthropic) helped with code, design and presentation materials.

Future Work

  • Real CO₂ data: replace Carbon Currents' simulated data with real gridded GEOS CO₂ and winds. The loader template is already in place.
  • More exhibits: add more datasets, such as sea surface temperature, lightning and night lights.
  • Better narration: record the narration with a high-quality neural voice, and translate it into more languages.
  • Testing with real users: run co-design and user testing with blind and low-vision communities to refine the sound rules and the navigation.
  • Touch and immersive versions: add vibration on phones, and build a VR or full-dome version for real planetariums.
  • Saving and sharing: let users save and share their own audio clips, so the music can be heard as a playlist.
